<reason>Both sides were sharp and format-compliant, but PRO built the cleaner path. B framed the motion as "may a worker be fired for reasons irrelevant to the job," then landed the two most damaging internal-contradiction hits: CON's praised anti-discrimination statutes are themselves one-sided mandates on association, and CON's pretext-evasion argument would equally defeat those same statutes. A's best counters either collapsed into B's frame — the gambling bookkeeper and reputational-risk hire are prospective job-connected reasons, which B's materiality/articulability test absorbs — or retreated to severance and safety nets, which B fairly characterized as cushioning arbitrary power rather than justifying it. B's closing reductio (the gay teacher and interracial marriage as "risks") showed A's forecast-based prudence cannot distinguish judgment from prejudice; A's reply ("that fight is won" via identity statutes) left politics and weekend life — the centerpiece cases — uncovered. A argued well throughout: the asymmetry frame, vagueness dilemma, and bookkeeper example were genuinely strong, and its pressure questions were pointed. B's blemishes were minor: a premature "silence is the concession" jab (answers were due the next turn) and a clipped rebuttal. On balance B won the decisive exchanges and made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The pretext-papering exchange: A argued the rule only manufactures paper rights since employers will paper files and workers lose slow lawsuits (A1.4, A2.6); B flipped it — evasion proves too much because it would void the discrimination statutes A praised, and "a remedy sometimes defeated beats powerlessness guaranteed" (B2.5, B4.3-4.4), turning A's strongest practical argument into B's best weighing line.</best_rebuttal>
